title: Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610 syllabus for 2026, 2027 and 2028 (version 3, published August 2026)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and subtopic headings, their numbering and the Core/Supplement split are transcribed from the official syllabus document (version 3). Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase and group the board's numbered statements; their numbering (subtopic code + .n) is ours and does not match the board's statement numbers. 'Supplement:' marks objectives that only Extended candidates are examined on. The 'Experimental skills and investigations' node records Section 4 (Practical assessment) and is not a numbered subject-content topic.
notes: Checked on 2026-10-07 against the official PDF (version 3, published August 2026; 'Use this syllabus for exams in 2026, 2027 and 2028'): all 21 topics and 61 subtopic headings, their numbering, the Core/Supplement split, the assessment overview and the list of practical contexts match. Version 3 changed only the assessment overview page and version 2 a weblink; Cambridge states there are no significant changes affecting teaching since the syllabus first examined in 2023.

Supplement-only subtopics (the Core column is empty): 8.4 Translocation, 17.2 Mitosis and 17.3 Meiosis. These nodes are linked to Papers 2 and 4. Within the other subtopics the Supplement statements are recorded as objectives starting 'Supplement:'; a node cannot restrict a concept by tier, so content on Supplement-only material should say so (lesson level 'extended').

Notable Supplement-only material inside shared subtopics: the five kingdoms, plant groups and viruses (1.3), DNA structure (4.1), the balanced equations for photosynthesis and respiration, limiting factors (6.1), bile, villi and the named enzymes pepsin, trypsin and maltase (7.3 to 7.5), double circulation (9.1), active and passive immunity, vaccination and cholera (10.1), ventilation mechanics (11.1), oxygen debt (12.3), the nephron and the liver (13.1), synapses (14.1), accommodation, rods and cones (14.2), glucagon, negative feedback, diabetes and temperature control (14.4), auxin (14.5), protein synthesis and haploid/diploid (17.1), test crosses, codominance and sex linkage (17.4), the nitrogen cycle (19.3), eutrophication (20.3) and fermenters, lactase and the genetic-modification process (21.2, 21.3).

The 'Experimental skills and investigations' node is ours: it represents Section 4 'Practical assessment' (assessment objective AO3, 20% of the qualification), which lists the experimental contexts and skills examined in Paper 5 (Practical Test) and Paper 6 (Alternative to Practical). The hazard codes listed in the syllabus (C, MH, HH, T, F, O, N) are for familiarity and are not assessed.

Topics 4, 5, 10, 11, 13 and 15 each have a single subtopic with the same heading (e.g. 4 and 4.1 'Biological molecules'), as in the document; the subtopic and 21.1 nodes have explicit slugs so that topic URLs stay unique.

Not in this syllabus (ZIMSEC-only concepts of the biology-o family are deliberately not covered here): branches of biology and careers, malnutrition diseases other than scurvy and rickets, crop pests and diseases, livestock productivity, malaria, bilharzia, tuberculosis and typhoid, the effects of smoking on the lungs, the ear, the skeleton, drug misuse, contraception, seed structure and dispersal, soil, and the management of natural and artificial ecosystems. Shared concepts may contain a few ZIMSEC-only details (e.g. brain regions, plant hormones other than auxin, named STIs other than HIV); items on them should be restricted with applies.

Paper facts (durations, marks, weightings, question types) are from the 'Assessment overview' and 'Details of the assessment' sections; calculators may be used in all papers ('Mathematical requirements').
overview: Cambridge IGCSE Biology develops knowledge and understanding of living organisms, from classification, cells, biological molecules and enzymes, through plant and human nutrition, transport, gas exchange, respiration, excretion, coordination, drugs and reproduction, to inheritance, variation and selection, ecology, human influences on ecosystems and biotechnology. It also develops the experimental skills of planning investigations, observing, measuring and recording, and analysing and evaluating results. All candidates study the Core content; Extended candidates also study the Supplement.
assessmentOverview: All candidates take three papers. Core candidates take Paper 1 (Multiple Choice, 45 minutes, 40 four-option questions, 40 marks, 30%) and Paper 3 (Theory, 1 hour 15 minutes, short-answer and structured questions, 80 marks, 50%) on the Core content and can be awarded grades C to G. Extended candidates take Paper 2 (Multiple Choice, 45 minutes, 40 marks, 30%) and Paper 4 (Theory, 1 hour 15 minutes, 80 marks, 50%) on the Core and Supplement content and can be awarded grades A* to G. Every candidate also takes either Paper 5 (Practical Test, 1 hour 15 minutes, 40 marks, 20%) or Paper 6 (Alternative to Practical, 1 hour, 40 marks, 20%), which test experimental skills. Assessment objectives: AO1 knowledge with understanding (50%), AO2 handling information and problem-solving (30%), AO3 experimental skills and investigations (20%). Calculators may be used in all papers.

routes.name: Core
routes.description: Papers 1 and 3, and either Paper 5 or Paper 6. Grades C to G are available.

routes.name: Extended
routes.description: Papers 2 and 4, and either Paper 5 or Paper 6. Grades A* to G are available.

topics.name: Characteristics and classification of living organisms

objectives.text: Describe the seven characteristics of living organisms (movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition), giving the precise meaning of each.

children.name: Concept and uses of classification systems

objectives.text: State that organisms are classified into groups by the features they share, and describe a species as a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Describe the binomial system, in which a species' scientific name is made of its genus and species.
Construct and use dichotomous keys based on features that can be identified.
Supplement: explain that classification aims to reflect evolutionary relationships and that DNA base sequences are used to classify organisms, closer relatives having more similar sequences.
State the main features used to place organisms in the animal and plant kingdoms.

State the main features of the vertebrate groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and the arthropod groups (myriapods, insects, arachnids, crustaceans), and use them to classify organisms.

Supplement: state the main features of the five kingdoms (animal, plant, fungus, prokaryote, protoctist) and of ferns and flowering plants (dicotyledons and monocotyledons), and use them to classify organisms.
Supplement: state that viruses consist of a protein coat and genetic material.
Describe and compare the structures of plant and animal cells (cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, chloroplasts, ribosomes, mitochondria, vacuoles) and identify them in diagrams and images.
Describe the structure of a bacterial cell (cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA, plasmids) and identify these structures in diagrams and images.
Describe the functions of the structures of plant, animal and bacterial cells, and state that new cells are made by the division of existing cells.
State the functions of ciliated cells, root hair cells, palisade mesophyll cells, neurones, red blood cells and gametes as specialised cells.
Describe what is meant by a cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism, using examples from the syllabus.
State and use the formula magnification = image size ÷ actual size to calculate magnification and the size of specimens in millimetres.
Supplement: convert measurements between millimetres and micrometres.

topics.name: Movement into and out of cells

objectives.text: Describe diffusion as the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient as a result of their random movement, powered by their kinetic energy.
State that some substances cross cell membranes by diffusion and describe why the diffusion of gases and solutes matters to organisms.
Investigate how surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance affect diffusion.
Describe the role of water as a solvent in digestion, excretion and transport.
State that water moves into and out of cells by osmosis through partially permeable membranes, and investigate osmosis using dialysis tubing.
Investigate and describe the effects on plant tissues of solutions of different concentrations, and state that plants are supported by the pressure of water inside cells pressing on the cell wall.
Supplement: describe osmosis in terms of water potential and explain its effects on plant cells using the terms turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis and flaccid.
Supplement: explain why water potential and osmosis matter in the uptake and loss of water by organisms.
Describe active transport as movement of particles through a membrane against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
Supplement: explain the importance of active transport, including ion uptake by root hairs, and state that protein carriers move the molecules or ions.
State which elements carbohydrates, fats and proteins contain.
State that starch, glycogen and cellulose are made from glucose, proteins from amino acids, and fats and oils from fatty acids and glycerol.
Describe the iodine, Benedict's, biuret, ethanol emulsion and DCPIP tests for starch, reducing sugars, proteins, fats and oils, and vitamin C.
Supplement: describe DNA as two strands coiled into a double helix, held together by bonds between pairs of bases that always pair A with T and C with G.
Describe a catalyst, and describe enzymes as proteins that act as biological catalysts in all metabolic reactions and are needed to keep reactions fast enough to sustain life.
Describe enzyme action in terms of an active site whose shape is complementary to the substrate, and the formation of products.
Investigate and describe how temperature and pH affect enzyme activity, including the optimum temperature and denaturation.
Supplement: explain enzyme action and specificity using the terms active site, enzyme-substrate complex, substrate and product, and the complementary fit of substrate and active site.
Supplement: explain the effect of temperature (kinetic energy, effective collisions, shape and fit, denaturation) and of pH (shape and fit, denaturation) on enzyme activity.
Describe photosynthesis, state its word equation, and state that chlorophyll is a green pigment in chloroplasts that transfers light energy into chemical energy for making carbohydrates.
Outline how the carbohydrates made in photosynthesis are used and stored: starch, cellulose, glucose for respiration, sucrose for transport in the phloem and nectar.
Explain why plants need nitrate ions to make amino acids and magnesium ions to make chlorophyll.
Investigate the need for chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide using suitable controls, and the effects of light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature on the rate of photosynthesis.
Investigate and describe gas exchange of an aquatic plant in light and dark using hydrogencarbonate indicator solution.
Supplement: state the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.
Supplement: identify and explain the limiting factors of photosynthesis in different environmental conditions.
Explain how the large surface area and thinness of most leaves are adaptations for photosynthesis.

Identify the structures of a dicotyledonous leaf (chloroplasts, cuticle, guard cells and stomata, upper and lower epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, air spaces, vascular bundles, xylem, phloem) and explain how each adapts the leaf for photosynthesis.
Describe a balanced diet.
State the main dietary sources and describe the importance of carbohydrates, fats and oils, proteins, vitamins C and D, calcium and iron, fibre and water.
State the dietary deficiencies that cause scurvy and rickets.
Identify the organs of the alimentary canal and the associated organs (salivary glands, pancreas, liver, gall bladder) in diagrams and images.
Describe the functions of these organs in ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion.
Describe physical digestion and state that it increases the surface area of food for enzymes.
Identify the types of human teeth, describe their structure and describe their functions in physical digestion.
Describe the role of the stomach in physical digestion.
Supplement: outline how bile emulsifies fats and oils, increasing the surface area for chemical digestion.
Describe chemical digestion and its role in producing small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.
Describe the functions of amylase, proteases and lipase, and state where each is secreted and where it acts.
Describe the functions of hydrochloric acid in gastric juice.
Supplement: describe the digestion of starch by amylase and maltase and of protein by pepsin and trypsin, and explain how bile neutralises the acidic mixture entering the duodenum.
State that nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine and that most water is absorbed there, with some absorbed in the colon.
Supplement: explain how villi and microvilli increase the surface area of the small intestine, describe the structure of a villus and the roles of its capillaries and lacteal.
State the functions of xylem and phloem and identify their positions in sections of roots, stems and leaves of non-woody dicotyledonous plants.
Supplement: relate the structure of xylem vessels (thick lignified walls, no cell contents, continuous tubes without cross walls) to their function.
Identify root hair cells, state their functions and state that their large surface area increases the uptake of water and mineral ions.
Outline the pathway of water through the root, stem and leaf, and investigate it in the parts above ground using a stain.
Describe transpiration as loss of water vapour from leaves by evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces into air spaces and diffusion out through the stomata.
Investigate and describe the effects of temperature and wind speed on the rate of transpiration.
Supplement: relate water vapour loss to the internal surface area of the air spaces and the size and number of stomata, and explain how transpiration pull moves a column of water up the xylem.
Supplement: explain the effects of temperature, wind speed and humidity on the rate of transpiration, and how and why wilting occurs.
Supplement: describe translocation of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources to sinks, and explain why a part of a plant may be a source at one time and a sink at another.
Describe a circulatory system as blood vessels with a pump and valves that keep blood flowing in one direction.
Supplement: describe the single circulation of a fish and the double circulation of a mammal, and explain the advantages of a double circulation.

Identify the structures of the mammalian heart (muscular wall, septum, atria, ventricles, one-way valves, coronary arteries), and state that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it.
State how the activity of the heart can be monitored (ECG, pulse rate, sounds of the valves) and investigate the effect of physical activity on heart rate.
Describe coronary heart disease and its risk factors, and discuss how diet and exercise reduce the risk.
Supplement: identify the atrioventricular and semilunar valves and explain the relative thickness of the walls of the chambers and the importance of the septum.
Supplement: describe how the heart works in terms of contraction of the atria and ventricles and the action of the valves, and explain the effect of physical activity on heart rate.
Describe the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries (wall thickness, lumen diameter, valves in veins) and state the functions of capillaries.
Identify the main blood vessels to and from the heart, lungs and kidneys.
Supplement: explain how the structures of arteries, veins and capillaries relate to blood pressure and their functions, and identify the hepatic artery, hepatic veins and hepatic portal vein.
List the components of blood, identify red and white blood cells in photomicrographs and diagrams, and state the functions of red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
State why blood clotting matters: it stops blood loss and keeps pathogens out.
Supplement: identify lymphocytes and phagocytes and state their functions, and describe clotting as the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin mesh.

children.name: Diseases and immunity
children.description: Active and passive immunity, vaccination and cholera are Supplement.

objectives.text: Describe a pathogen and a transmissible disease, and state how pathogens are transmitted directly and indirectly.
Describe the body's defences: skin, hairs in the nose, mucus, stomach acid and white blood cells.
Explain how a clean water supply, hygienic food preparation, good personal hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment control the spread of disease.
Supplement: describe active immunity, antigens and antibodies, and outline how vaccination gives long-term immunity through memory cells and controls the spread of disease.
Supplement: explain passive immunity, including antibodies passed across the placenta and in breast milk, and state that it produces no memory cells.
Supplement: describe cholera as a bacterial disease spread in contaminated water and explain how its toxin causes diarrhoea, dehydration and loss of ions.
Describe the features of gas exchange surfaces in humans and identify the parts of the breathing system.
Investigate and describe the differences in oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour between inspired and expired air, using limewater to test for carbon dioxide.
Investigate and describe the effects of physical activity on the rate and depth of breathing.

Supplement: identify the internal and external intercostal muscles, state the function of cartilage in the trachea, and explain how the ribs, intercostal muscles and diaphragm cause the volume and pressure changes that ventilate the lungs.

Supplement: explain the differences between inspired and expired air, and explain how increased carbon dioxide in the blood, detected by the brain, increases the rate and depth of breathing during exercise.
Supplement: explain how goblet cells, mucus and ciliated cells protect the breathing system from pathogens and particles.
List the ways in which living organisms use the energy released by respiration.
Investigate and describe the effect of temperature on respiration in yeast.
Describe aerobic respiration and state its word equation.
Supplement: state the balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration.
Describe anaerobic respiration, state that it releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration, and state its word equations in yeast and in muscles during vigorous exercise.
Supplement: state the balanced equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast, and describe how lactic acid causes an oxygen debt and how the debt is removed after exercise.
State what the lungs excrete (carbon dioxide) and what the kidneys excrete (urea, excess water and excess ions), and identify the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra.
Supplement: identify the cortex and medulla of the kidney and outline how a nephron filters the blood and reabsorbs all the glucose, some ions and most of the water to form urine.
Supplement: describe how the liver assimilates amino acids into proteins and deaminates excess amino acids to form urea, and explain why urea must be excreted.
State that electrical impulses travel along neurones, describe the central and peripheral nervous systems and the role of the nervous system in coordination and regulation.
Identify sensory, relay and motor neurones, and describe a simple reflex arc and a reflex action.
State that a synapse is the junction where two neurones meet.
Supplement: describe the structure of a synapse and the events that pass an impulse across it, and state that synapses make impulses travel in one direction only.
Describe sense organs as groups of receptor cells that respond to specific stimuli.
Identify the parts of the eye, describe their functions and explain the pupil reflex.
Supplement: explain the pupil reflex using the circular and radial muscles of the iris, and explain accommodation using the ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments and lens shape.
Supplement: describe the distribution and functions of rods and cones and identify the fovea and state its function.
Describe a hormone, and identify the adrenal glands, pancreas, testes and ovaries and state the hormones they secrete.
Describe the effects of adrenaline in 'fight or flight' situations and compare nervous and hormonal control.
Supplement: state that the pancreas secretes glucagon and describe how adrenaline raises blood glucose concentration and heart rate.

children.name: Homeostasis
children.description: Core: the meaning of homeostasis and the effect of insulin; everything else is Supplement.

objectives.text: Describe homeostasis and state that insulin decreases blood glucose concentration.
Supplement: explain negative feedback around a set point, describe the control of blood glucose by the liver, insulin and glucagon, and outline the treatment of Type 1 diabetes.

Supplement: identify the structures of the skin and describe how body temperature is kept constant by insulation, sweating, shivering, the brain, and vasodilation and vasoconstriction of arterioles supplying skin capillaries.
Describe gravitropism and phototropism and investigate them in shoots and roots.
Supplement: explain phototropism and gravitropism of a shoot as chemical control of growth by auxin.
Describe a drug, describe the use of antibiotics to treat bacterial infections and state that antibiotics do not affect viruses.
State that antibiotic resistance in some bacteria makes antibiotic treatment less effective.
Supplement: explain how using antibiotics only when essential limits the development of resistant bacteria such as MRSA.
Describe asexual reproduction and identify examples in diagrams, images and information.
Supplement: discuss the advantages and disadvantages of asexual reproduction for wild populations and for crop production.
Describe sexual reproduction and fertilisation.
Supplement: state that gamete nuclei are haploid and the zygote nucleus is diploid, and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of sexual reproduction for wild populations and for crop production.
Identify, draw and state the functions of the parts of an insect-pollinated flower, and identify and describe the anthers and stigmas of a wind-pollinated flower.
Distinguish the pollen grains and describe the structural adaptations of insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers, and describe pollination.
State that fertilisation occurs when a pollen nucleus fuses with a nucleus in an ovule, and investigate the conditions needed for seeds to germinate.
Supplement: describe self-pollination and cross-pollination and discuss their effects on a population.
Supplement: describe the growth of the pollen tube and its entry into the ovule, followed by fertilisation.
Identify the parts of the male and female reproductive systems and state their functions.
Describe fertilisation, explain the adaptive features of sperm and egg cells, and compare male and female gametes.
State that the zygote forms an embryo that implants in the lining of the uterus, and state the functions of the umbilical cord, placenta, amniotic sac and amniotic fluid.
Supplement: describe the exchange of substances between mother and fetus across the placenta, and state that some pathogens and toxins can cross it.
Describe the roles of testosterone and oestrogen in secondary sexual characteristics at puberty, and describe the menstrual cycle in terms of changes in the ovaries and the uterus lining.
Supplement: describe where oestrogen and progesterone are produced in the menstrual cycle and in pregnancy, and explain the roles of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone.
Describe a sexually transmitted infection, state that HIV causes an STI that may lead to AIDS, describe how HIV is transmitted and explain how the spread of STIs is controlled.
State that chromosomes are made of DNA containing genes, and define a gene and an allele.
Describe the inheritance of sex in humans using X and Y chromosomes.
Supplement: explain how the base sequence of a gene determines the amino acid sequence and shape of a protein, and how DNA controls cell function through protein production.
Supplement: explain how a protein is made using mRNA and ribosomes, and why cells express only some of their genes.
Supplement: describe haploid and diploid nuclei and state that a human diploid cell has 23 pairs of chromosomes.
Supplement: describe mitosis as nuclear division giving genetically identical cells, state its roles, and state that chromosomes are copied before mitosis and the copies separate during it.
Supplement: describe stem cells as unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to give cells that can become specialised.
Supplement: state that meiosis produces gametes and describe it as a reduction division from diploid to haploid that gives genetically different cells.

children.name: Monohybrid inheritance
children.description: Test crosses, codominance and sex linkage are Supplement.

objectives.text: Describe inheritance, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous, pure-breeding, dominant allele and recessive allele.
Interpret pedigree diagrams for the inheritance of a characteristic.
Use genetic diagrams and Punnett squares to predict the results of monohybrid crosses and calculate 1 : 1 and 3 : 1 phenotypic ratios.
Supplement: explain how a test cross identifies an unknown genotype.
Supplement: describe codominance and explain the inheritance of the ABO blood groups.
Supplement: describe sex linkage, using red-green colour blindness as an example, and use genetic diagrams for crosses involving codominance or sex linkage.
Describe variation, and distinguish continuous and discontinuous variation, their examples and their causes.
Investigate and describe examples of continuous and discontinuous variation.
Describe mutation as genetic change that forms new alleles, and state that ionising radiation and some chemicals increase the mutation rate.
Supplement: describe gene mutation as a random change in the base sequence of DNA and state the sources of genetic variation in populations.
Describe an adaptive feature and interpret images or information about a species to describe its adaptive features.
Supplement: explain how hydrophytes and xerophytes are adapted to their environments.
Describe natural selection.
Describe selective breeding and outline how it improves crop plants and domesticated animals over many generations, applying this to given contexts.
Supplement: describe adaptation as a result of natural selection, describe antibiotic-resistant bacteria as an example, and outline the differences between natural and artificial selection.
State that the Sun is the principal source of energy for biological systems and describe how energy flows through organisms and is eventually transferred to the environment.
Describe, construct and interpret food chains and food webs using the terms producer, consumer (primary to quaternary), herbivore, carnivore, decomposer and trophic level.
Use food chains and webs to describe the effects of overharvesting and of introducing foreign species.
Draw, describe and interpret pyramids of numbers and biomass, and discuss the advantages of a pyramid of biomass.

Supplement: draw and interpret pyramids of energy and explain why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient, why food chains are short and why eating crops is more energy-efficient than eating livestock.
Describe the carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, formation of fossil fuels and combustion.
Supplement: describe the nitrogen cycle and state the roles of microorganisms in decomposition, nitrification, nitrogen fixation and denitrification.
Describe a population, a community and an ecosystem.
State the factors that affect the rate of population growth, identify the phases of a sigmoid growth curve and interpret graphs of population growth.
Supplement: explain the factors that lead to each phase of the sigmoid growth curve, including limiting factors.
Describe how agricultural machinery, chemical fertilisers, insecticides, herbicides and selective breeding have increased food production.
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of large-scale monocultures and of intensive livestock production.
Describe biodiversity and the reasons for habitat destruction, and state that humans can harm habitats by altering food chains and webs.
Explain the undesirable effects of deforestation.
Describe the effects of untreated sewage and excess fertiliser on aquatic ecosystems and of non-biodegradable plastics on aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems.
Describe the sources and effects of air pollution by methane and carbon dioxide, limited to the enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change.
Supplement: explain the sequence of events in eutrophication, from extra nitrate to the death of organisms that need dissolved oxygen.
Describe a sustainable resource and state that forests and fish stocks can be conserved and managed sustainably.
Explain why organisms become endangered or extinct and describe how endangered species can be conserved.
Supplement: explain how forests and fish stocks can be conserved and describe the reasons for conservation programmes.
Supplement: describe the use of artificial insemination and IVF in captive breeding, and explain the risks to a species when a small population loses genetic variation.
State why bacteria are useful in biotechnology and genetic modification: they reproduce quickly and can make complex molecules.
Supplement: discuss why bacteria are useful, including the few ethical concerns over growing them and the presence of plasmids.
Describe the role of anaerobic respiration in yeast in producing ethanol for biofuels and in bread-making.
Describe the use of pectinase in fruit juice production, and investigate and describe the use of biological washing powders containing enzymes.
Supplement: explain the use of lactase to produce lactose-free milk.
Supplement: describe how fermenters are used to produce insulin, penicillin and mycoprotein, and explain the conditions that must be controlled in a fermenter.
Describe genetic modification and outline examples: human proteins made by bacteria, and crop plants given herbicide resistance, insect-pest resistance or improved nutritional qualities.
Supplement: outline how bacteria are genetically modified to make a human protein, using restriction enzymes, sticky ends, plasmids and DNA ligase.
Supplement: discuss the advantages and disadvantages of genetically modifying crops such as soya, maize and rice.

topics.name: Experimental skills and investigations
topics.description: Not a numbered subject-content topic: Section 4 'Practical assessment' (assessment objective AO3) lists the experimental skills and contexts examined in Paper 5 (Practical Test) and Paper 6 (Alternative to Practical). Practical-skills content is tagged here.

objectives.text: Select and use techniques, apparatus and materials safely, including food tests and testing pH, and describe and explain hazards and safety precautions.

Plan experiments: identify the independent and dependent variables, explain which variables to keep constant and how, choose a suitable range of values, include a control and describe how results will be recorded and processed.
Make and record observations and measurements to an appropriate precision in suitable tables, and make clear labelled drawings of specimens, calculating magnification or actual size.
Process and present data (calculations, graphs, interpolation, gradients), identify anomalous results and draw conclusions justified by the data.
Evaluate methods and data, identify sources of error, suggest improvements and use representative sampling methods.
